title: HTTP Status Codes: The Dense Notes Edition
summary: A page-per-concept carousel covering what each status family means, how to choose between 400/422/409, retry semantics with Retry-After, and idempotency expectations for safe API design.

chapters.title: The Status Code Mental Model
points: Every HTTP response carries a 3-digit status: first digit = class, next two = specific code
1xx informational, 2xx success, 3xx redirection, 4xx client error, 5xx server error
Codes are semantics, not just numbers — clients make decisions based on the class alone
The reason phrase (e.g. 'Not Found') is advisory; only the code is contractual
Unknown codes within a class should be handled like the class: unknown 4xx = client error
Servers may send codes not in the RFC registry — extensibility is part of the spec
Status + body + headers form one message: a 200 with an error payload is a design smell
Rule of thumb: 4xx says 'the request is broken', 5xx says 'the server failed on a valid request'

chapters.title: 2xx — Success, Precisely
points: 200 OK: general success; body depends on the method (resource for GET, result for POST)
201 Created: new resource made; set Location header to the new resource URI
204 No Content: success with empty body — ideal for DELETE and PUT confirmations
202 Accepted: request queued for async processing; client must poll or be notified later
206 Partial Content: only with Range headers; the backbone of resumable downloads
Using 200 for everything breaks Location semantics and forces clients to parse bodies
204 must have no body — sending one confuses some clients and proxies
202 means 'not done yet': don't return 202 for work completed synchronously
304 lives with redirections but means success: 'your cached copy is still valid'

chapters.title: 3xx — Redirects Done Right
points: 301 Moved Permanently: cached aggressively by browsers; method can change to GET
302 Found: temporary, but historically methods got rewritten to GET
303 See Other: explicitly says 'fetch the new URI with GET' — use after POST
307/308: temporary/permanent redirects that preserve method and body — the strict successors to 302/301
304 Not Modified: conditional GET (If-None-Match) — no body, saves bandwidth
Redirect loops: same-origin chains must terminate; cap redirects clientside (~20) and serverside
APIs should usually redirect once or not at all — internal rewrites belong in the server
Never redirect with credentials/headers you wouldn't leak to the target host
Rule: need the method preserved? 307/308. Sending a user after a form POST? 303

chapters.title: 4xx — The Client's Fault, Named
points: 400 Bad Request: malformed syntax the server can't parse — bad JSON, bad encoding
401 Unauthorized (really 'unauthenticated'): missing/invalid credentials; must include WWW-Authenticate
403 Forbidden: authenticated but not allowed; do not re-authenticate
404 Not Found: resource doesn't exist; 410 Gone: it existed and was deliberately removed
405 Method Not Allowed: verb unsupported on that URI; must include Allow header
415 Unsupported Media Type: request body format rejected
429 Too Many Requests: rate limiting; pair with Retry-After (next chapter)
Choice rule: can't parse it → 400; who are you → 401; may you → 403; does it exist → 404
404 vs 403 leak trade-off: returning 403 on private resources confirms they exist

chapters.title: 400 vs 422 vs 409 — The Classic Interview
points: 400: the request is structurally broken — server can't even parse it to evaluate it
422 Unprocessable Content: well-formed but semantically invalid — fails validation/business rules
409 Conflict: the request contradicts current server state — would create an inconsistency
Malformed JSON → 400; email field missing → 422; username already taken → 409
Concurrency conflict: If-Match/ETag mismatch on PUT → 412 Precondition Failed (or 409)
409 should describe what state conflicts so the client can resolve and retry
422 body should carry field-level errors: {"errors": [{"field": "email", "issue": "invalid"}]}
Historical note: 422 came from WebDAV; 411/422 refinements now in RFC 9110 ('Unprocessable Content')
Overusing 400 for validation hides which fields failed — clients can't show helpful errors
Stale-state operations (order already shipped) → 409, not 422: it's state, not input
Decision tree: parseable? no→400 · valid against schema? no→422 · consistent with state? no→409

chapters.title: 5xx — The Server's Fault
points: 500 Internal Server Error: unhandled exception; never leak stack traces to clients
501 Not Implemented: server doesn't support the method/feature at all (rare, honest)
502 Bad Gateway / 504 Gateway Timeout: upstream/proxy failures — the classic microservices codes
503 Service Unavailable: temporary overload or maintenance; signal it with Retry-After
503 is the one 5xx that invites a retry — 500 generally doesn't (or shouldn't, blindly)
Choose 503 over 500 when shedding load deliberately: it tells clients the failure is temporary
Map upstream errors: upstream 4xx → pass through; upstream 5xx/timeout → your 502/504
5xx are your monitoring SLI: spike = incident; 4xx spikes usually mean client bugs or abuse
Anti-pattern: catching all exceptions and returning 400 — you've hidden server bugs as client faults

chapters.title: Retry-After and Retry Semantics
points: Retry-After header: tells the client when to try again — valid on 503, 429, and 301/302... redirects (rarely used there)
Two formats: HTTP-date ('Retry-After: Wed, 21 Oct 2025 07:28:00 GMT') or seconds ('Retry-After: 120')
429 + Retry-After = rate-limit contract; clients that ignore it get blocked harder
Servers: emit Retry-After on deliberate throttling and planned maintenance windows
Clients: respect it as a floor — retrying sooner amplifies the overload (retry storm)
Combine with exponential backoff + jitter for codes without Retry-After (500s, timeouts)
Only retry idempotent operations automatically, or use idempotency keys (next chapter)
Honor max retry budgets (e.g. 3 attempts) and circuit-break after consecutive failures
Headers that shape retries: Retry-After (when), ETag/If-Match (what version), RateLimit-* (forecast)

chapters.title: Idempotency: Which Methods Promise What
points: Idempotent = same request N times leaves the same state as once — independent of the count
Safe = no state change at all (GET, HEAD, OPTIONS); a subset of idempotent
GET/PUT/DELETE are idempotent; POST and PATCH are not guaranteed
GET can still log, cache, or fire analytics — 'safe' means resource state, not zero side effects
Retrying non-idempotent POST risks double-charging — the motivation for idempotency keys
Idempotency-Key header: client generates a unique key per logical operation; server dedupes and replays the stored response
Key lifecycle: store key+response until client confirms or TTL expires (commonly 24h); concurrent duplicates → 409 or hold-then-replay
PUT is idempotent because it sets state ('set x=5' twice = same), not because it's a 'update verb'
DELETE is idempotent: second call returns 404 but state is unchanged — success semantics ≠ idempotency
Rule: any code path that can time out after committing (payments!) must be safe to retry

chapters.title: Design Cheat Sheet & Closing Summary
points: Pick the most specific code; the class is the contract, the code is the documentation
CRUD mapping: create→201+Location, read→200/304, update→200/204, delete→204/404
Validation ladder: 400 (unparseable) → 422 (invalid) → 409 (conflicts with state)
Auth ladder: 401 (who are you) → 403 (not allowed) → 404 (hide existence)
Retry matrix: 429/503 honor Retry-After; 500/504 backoff + jitter; 4xx (except 409/429/408) don't retry
Every 2xx/4xx/5xx decision should be provable from the request alone — no guessing for the client
Status codes are for HTTP-level semantics; domain outcomes can live in bodies, but never contradict the code
Log both sides: server logs 5xx as errors, 4xx as warnings; alert on 5xx rate, investigate 4xx spikes
Test checklist: one test per code you return, including Retry-After presence and idempotent replay
Golden rule: a client that only reads the status class should still behave correctly
